general_notes.general_notes:
This was a large-scale, comprehensive benchmarking study that provides a robust, optimised pipeline for normative modelling of brain morphometry. The full list of the 87 datasets used in the reference cohort is available in Appendix 2.


NONCANONICAL_DATA:
- study_id: "Ge2024"
- reference_file_names: "Ge2024.pdf.md; Ge2024_sup1.xlsx.md; Ge2024_sup2.xlsx.md; Ge2024_sup3.xlsx.md; Ge2024_sup4.xlsx.md; Ge2024_sup5.xlsx.md; Ge2024_sup6.pdf.md"
- author_journal_year: "Ge et al., Lancet Digit Health, 2024"
- title: "Normative modelling of brain morphometry across the lifespan with CentileBrain: algorithm benchmarking and model optimisation"
- doi: "NR"
- study_objective: "To benchmark eight common normative modelling algorithms and propose an optimal modelling pipeline for brain morphometry across the lifespan. The study also aimed to test the clinical utility of the optimised models in a case-control sample of early psychosis patients."
- study_design: "Cross-sectional"
- study_design_other: "-"
- dataset_name: "Aggregated multi-site dataset from 87 cohorts, including ENIGMA, ABCD, HCP, and UK Biobank. The full list is in Appendix 2."
- hc_n: 37407
- hc_age: "3-90 years (mean 39.88, SD 23.47)"
- hc_sex: "F 19964 (53.4%), M 17443 (46.6%)"
- imaging_modality: "T1-weighted MRI"
- analysis_level: "ROI-level (68 cortical thickness and surface area regions from Desikan-Killiany atlas, 14 subcortical volumes from Aseg atlas)"
- preprocessing_pipeline: "FreeSurfer (versions 5.1, 5.3, 6.0, 7.1, 7.2)"
- quality_checking: "Yes"
- quality_checking_detail: "Quality control was performed using the ENIGMA consortium protocols, which include visual inspection and quantitative checks. The Qoala-T tool was used for T1-weighted images. Outlier removal was based on the Euler number (EN) and the interquartile range (IQR) of the median EN per site."
- site_effect_handling: "Other"
- site_effect_handling_detail: "The study compared two approaches for handling site effects: 1) including site as a random factor in the model (for LMM and GAMLSS) and 2) harmonising data prior to modelling using ComBat-GAM. The top-performing algorithm (MFPR) showed similar performance with both methods, so ComBat-GAM was chosen for the final pipeline for its flexibility."
- model_origin: "New"
- model_origin_detail: "-"
- modeling_method: "The study benchmarked eight algorithms: Linear model (LM), Linear mixed-effects model (LMM), Bayesian linear regression (BLR), Bayesian linear mixed-effects model (BLMM), Generalized additive models for location, scale and shape (GAMLSS), Hierarchical Bayesian regression (HBR), Probabilistic clinical map (PCM), and Multivariate fractional polynomial regression (MFPR). MFPR was identified as the optimal algorithm."
- software_tool: "R (packages: lm, lme4, rstanarm, gamlss, mfp), Python (PCNtoolkit)"
- response_variable: "Cortical thickness, cortical surface area, and subcortical volumes."
- predictor_variables: "Age, Sex, and global neuroimaging measures (intracranial volume (ICV) for subcortical volumes, mean cortical thickness for regional thickness, and total surface area for regional surface area)."
- predictor_effects: "Age was modelled using non-linear fractional polynomials. Global neuroimaging measures were included as linear covariates. Sex was handled by fitting separate models for males and females."
- nm_vldtn_handle_ns: {"evaluation": "Yes", "description": "Site effects were explicitly handled by comparing ComBat-GAM harmonisation and including site as a random effect. Other covariates (age, sex, global brain measures) were included in the models."}
- nm_vldtn_same_domain_nonindep: {"evaluation": "Yes", "description": "5-fold cross-validation was performed on the training set (80% of the data) to evaluate model performance during the algorithm benchmarking phase."}
- nm_vldtn_same_domain_indep: {"evaluation": "Yes", "description": "Models were trained on 80% of the data and evaluated on a held-out test set (the remaining 20% of the data), which is an independent, same-domain validation."}
- nm_vldtn_diff_domain: {"evaluation": "Yes", "description": "The temporal stability of the Z-scores was assessed on two external, longitudinal datasets (SLIM and QTAB) which were not used for training the models. This serves as a form of different-domain validation, testing the model on data with different characteristics (longitudinal vs. cross-sectional)."}
- clinical_dataset: "Human Connectome Project-Early Psychosis (HCP-EP)"
- diseases_studied: "Early Psychosis"
- clinical_groups_n: "Early Psychosis: 91, Healthy Controls: 57"
- clinical_groups_age: "16.67-35.67 years (for the whole HCP-EP cohort)"
- clinical_groups_sex: "NR (Not reported separately for clinical vs. control within the paper, but the total sample was 48 F / 100 M)"
- deviation_metric: "Z-score, defined as (y - ŷ) / RMSEm, where y is the observed value, ŷ is the predicted value, and RMSEm is the root mean square error of the model."
- association_analysis: "1. Diagnostic Classification: A Support Vector Classifier (SVC) was used to predict diagnosis (patient vs. control) from both raw brain measures and Z-scores. 2. Symptom Severity Prediction: Ridge regression was used to predict the severity of positive and negative symptoms from both raw measures and Z-scores."
- key_findings_brief: "Multivariate Fractional Polynomial Regression (MFPR) was the best-performing normative modeling algorithm, and its derived Z-scores improved diagnostic classification of early psychosis patients compared to raw data, but did not improve symptom severity prediction."
- key_findings_detailed: "The study benchmarked eight algorithms and found MFPR to be optimal in terms of accuracy (lowest MAE) and computational efficiency. The optimal model included non-linear age effects, sex-specific models, and global brain measures as covariates. Model performance was found to plateau at a sample size of around 3000. In a clinical application, Z-scores from the MFPR model significantly improved the classification of early psychosis patients (AUC = 0.63) compared to using raw neuroimaging data (AUC = 0.49). However, Z-scores did not show a significant advantage over raw data in predicting the severity of positive or negative symptoms."
- key_limitations: "The authors note several limitations, including: 1) the cross-sectional nature of the primary dataset, which limits the ability to model true developmental trajectories; 2) a relative lack of data for young and middle-aged adults compared to other age groups; and 3) the need for further validation in more diverse ancestral and clinical populations."
- application_notes: "The study provides the trained models, analysis scripts, and a web-based tool called 'CentileBrain' for users to compute Z-scores for their own data. The optimal pipeline involved using ComBat-GAM for site harmonisation followed by the MFPR model with sex-specific fits."
